messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 39
- Gender: Female
- Ethnicity: Oceania
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: Park Ranger
- Trauma Type: Relief worker in war zone
- Pcl5: 43

At 39, she has spent most of her adult life working outdoors, and even now, as a park ranger, she says she trusts the bush more than she trusts most rooms. In the park she can read weather, animal tracks, and the shape of a day by the way light moves across the ridgeline. It is harder for her to read herself. When she begins talking about the year she spent overseas as a relief worker in a war zone, she does so carefully, as if stepping onto ground that may still be mined.

She is married now, and when she speaks about her husband there is warmth and embarrassment mixed together, because she knows how much of this life he has had to absorb without fully understanding it. Before she took the relief assignment, she had been the person in every emergency who stayed steady. She was practical, competent, the one others followed. She says she went because she believed she could help and because it seemed wrong, from the safety of home, to do nothing.

At first, she tells it as work. Distributing food. Checking water access. Driving between damaged neighborhoods with local staff who taught her which streets were safer and which sounds meant run. She learned quickly to sort terror into tasks. Then one afternoon a convoy ahead of hers was hit. She remembers the sequence in fragments rather than as a whole: the crack that did not sound real at first, dust lifting into the air, people shouting in two languages, a child’s shoe in the road, one of her colleagues pulling her down so hard her knees bruised on concrete. What comes back most strongly is not only the fear that she would die, but the shock of seeing civilians move through catastrophe as if this had become ordinary. She spent hours after that helping where she could, hands shaking while she bandaged people she could not save.

There were other incidents after that, which seem to layer over one another in her memory: mortar fire at night, the smell of burning plastic, a hospital corridor with too many bodies and not enough sheets. She stopped sleeping properly there. Even when she closed her eyes, her body stayed alert, waiting. She began startling at footsteps outside her quarters and keeping her boots on beside the bed. She told herself this was adaptation, not distress. Everyone around her was living the same reality. She kept working, became more efficient, and inwardly more numb.

When she came home, people praised her. They asked for stories over dinner, the brave kind, the meaningful kind. She found she could not tell the truth in the shape they wanted. The supermarket undid her before any conversation did: too much choice, bright lights, people drifting casually in aisles while she tracked exits and watched hands. A pallet dropping in the stockroom sent her to the floor before she knew what she was doing. She laughed it off afterward, humiliated by the silence around her.

She eventually returned to conservation work and became a park ranger, a job that suits the part of her that still needs competence and movement. Out on patrol she is calm. She knows how to manage risk, how to respond if a hiker is injured or a fire line shifts. Colleagues see her as capable, maybe a little intense. They do not see what it costs her to patrol remote areas after a helicopter passes overhead, or how certain smells—diesel, hot metal, smoke hanging low—can pull her out of the present so abruptly that she has to stop walking and place a hand on a tree until the ground feels like her own country again.

At home, the war enters in smaller ways. Her husband has learned not to come up behind her in the kitchen. She checks locks twice before bed and keeps her phone charged, flashlight on the bedside table. Sleep is thin and easily broken. Some nights she wakes already standing, heart pounding, having dreamed she is back in the compound hearing incoming fire. On those mornings she is ashamed and irritable. She snaps over nothing, then withdraws because she cannot bear being touched when her nerves are lit up. She hates that this distance has become part of their marriage, especially because she also fears being alone.

She avoids news footage from conflict zones, but avoidance has made her world smaller than she wants to admit. Community events feel unpredictable. Crowds drain her. Even at family gatherings she catches herself scanning faces, windows, exits, calculating where she would move if something happened. She knows this makes no sense in the moment, yet her body acts before reason can catch up. There are also stretches of blankness around the worst days overseas, and this unsettles her; she worries about what is buried there.

What troubles her most is not only fear, but the way the experience changed her understanding of other people. She still believes in service, still cares deeply about the land and the public who move through it, but some part of her remains braced against sudden harm. She misses the ease she once had. In the park, at dawn, when the air is cold and the tracks are fresh in the dirt, she sometimes feels briefly restored. Then a distant bang echoes through the valley, and she is back inside the old alertness, carrying a war into a landscape she once thought could hold anything.
